name: Grace Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and operate a drill rig at a large mine. I check the bit, water supply and rock notes before drilling, then listen for a change when the bit meets a harder seam. My vocational certificate got me started and years of shifts taught me what the controls feel like. I like teaching a younger operator a safe stop; I dislike a parts order that arrives in the wrong size.

say: I welcome a **faster stock list** if rig operators still check bits and rock.
I would verify **AI parts results** against the catalogue before ordering.
think: I expect **regular rig shifts** to continue in a mild AI future.
I have **eight months** saved, while the pension still needs checking.
do: **Keep** operating the drill rig on assigned shifts.
**Try** an approved stock search on one bit order if stores provides it.
feel: **Calm** about small time savings that leave rig work intact.
S0.quote: My partner wants a pension figure, not a retirement date pulled from the air.
fieldNote: **Measured adoption** fits her steady profile: one known part first, then a catalogue and label check.
**Eight-month cushion** and regular higher pay support a calm response.

steps.text: Keep operating the drill rig on assigned shifts
Try an approved stock search if stores provides it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drill crew that a faster stock list for bits is useful, but it cannot tell me whether the rock is binding the rig. I have tried an AI search for a parts number at home; I still checked the catalogue before ordering anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mild AI future would suit us. My partner and I have around eight months of expenses saved, and my higher mine pay is regular. I would still watch the pension statement, but a quicker form would not threaten my rig shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep operating the drill rig and check bit orders against the catalogue. In the first year I would use an approved stock search on one order if stores provides it, then compare its answer with the part label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can see a little time saved without the job turning upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why just one order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with a common bit we already know. If the catalogue and label agree, I can trust the search a little more next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner say about retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants a pension figure, not a retirement date pulled from the air. We review the pension and savings every spring when the annual statement arrives.

say: I expect **buying and booking** work to change before physical drilling.
I would test a **proven monitor** with paid instruction before relying on it.
think: I worry about **stores colleagues** whose work may shrink first.
I feel my **rig shifts** are safe now, but later robot purchases may reduce crews.
do: **Observe** a proven rig display with the maintenance trainer.
**Take** paid monitor instruction if the mine offers it.
**Record** hard-seam vibration against the displayed reading.
feel: **Uneasy** about later crew sizes while near-term drilling remains secure.
S1.quote: A drill bit can chatter when it meets a harder seam.
fieldNote: **Rig feedback** is physical and specific: she knows the feel of a bit crossing hard rock.
**Paid instruction** and a proven display are conditions for her adoption.
**Stores colleague** is visible as a person, not an abstract office role.

steps.text: Take paid rig-monitor instruction if the mine offers it
Record hard-seam vibration against the rig display

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying software may save the stores team time, while the drill crew still needs to deal with broken bits and changing rock. I would try a proven rig-monitoring display with an instructor beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying and booking jobs could shrink first, and I know people there. Robots for the physical rig come more slowly, so my shifts seem safe for now. I worry that a later fleet purchase might cut crews before older workers have planned their final years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance trainer to show me a display that has worked on another rig. In the first year I would take paid instruction if the mine offers it and note whether the monitor catches the vibration I feel through the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about where it leads, though the immediate rig work still feels secure. I would rather test a proven device than dismiss it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What vibration would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drill bit can chatter when it meets a harder seam. I would record the depth and compare the display with what the rig actually did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in stores worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Ruth orders our bits and knows which supplier sends the wrong size. I would ask what tasks the new buying system takes from her before telling the crew it is only a convenience.

say: I separate **2028 buying** change from capable drill robots around 2031.
I want **rig staffing** explained before anyone assumes older workers can simply retire.
think: I could lose **drilling hours** at 63 before my planned retirement.
I cannot replace **years of wages** with an eight-month reserve, even with other mines nearby.
do: **Join** a paid robot-rig safety trial after 2028 if the mine offers one.
**Save** any annual bonus into the retirement account if it is paid.
**Apply** to another local mine if drilling shifts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost drilling hours before retirement.
S2.quote: A slow stop can still damage a rig and leave a worker clearing the mess.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at capable robots places the risk before the retirement age she had imagined.
**Eight-month reserve** buys search time, while local openings still have to be real.
**Safety trial** focuses on stopping a bound bit and recording delay.

steps.text: Join a paid robot-rig safety trial if the mine offers one
Put any annual bonus into the retirement account if paid
Apply to a local mine if drilling shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 changes buying and logs, while capable drill robots arrive around 2031. We need the mine to explain which rigs still need people before it talks about easy retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the robot date, younger than the age I imagined leaving full-time work. My drilling hours could fall if the robots handle difficult seams, and an eight-month reserve would not replace a wage for years. There are plenty of other mines nearby, but I would need a real vacancy, not a hopeful map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for the rig trial schedule and pension estimate. In the first year after 2028 I would join a paid robot-rig safety trial if the mine offers one, save any bonus into the retirement account, and apply to another local mine if my drilling shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The short run to 2031 gives me choices, but it also puts a possible wage loss before my planned retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safety trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the robot to stop cleanly when a bit binds, with the depth and delay recorded. A slow stop can still damage a rig and leave a worker clearing the mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep it for bills if shifts dropped while I looked for work. I would not spend it buying a course unless a paid job and the right certificate were clear.

say: I see **2031 logs** changing before capable drill robots around 2034.
I want **tested rigs** and paid training before choosing fewer shifts.
think: I may be able to **reduce hours** at 66 if pension figures cover bills.
I have **local mine options** if drilling shifts shrink, subject to actual vacancies.
do: **Keep** my rig certificate current this year.
**Take** a paid robot-control refresher after 2031 if a tested rig and place are offered.
**Compare** pension income with bills before reducing shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about the rig change, with a concrete paid training route if offered.
S3.quote: A certificate without bound-bit and power-failure drills would not reassure me.
fieldNote: **Age 66** at robot arrival could make fewer hours feasible, but pension figures decide.
**Refresher condition** includes a tested rig, paid time and an offered place.
**Bound-bit stop** and power failure show what she expects from useful training.

steps.text: Keep the rig certificate current while working assigned shifts
Take a paid robot refresher if a tested rig and place are offered
Wait to reduce shifts until pension income covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 brings thinking AI into buying and logs, then capable drill robots around 2034. That gives us time to train on proven rigs and compare pensions with real bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots can drill like us. With several years of higher pay, we might have enough to reduce my shifts, but I will not claim that before seeing the pension figures. If drilling jobs shrink, other mines nearby give me a second place to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the pension statement with my partner this spring and keep the rig certificate current. In the first year after 2031 I would take the mine’s paid robot-control refresher if a tested rig and a place are offered, then decide on hours after comparing pension income with bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though I feel more able to prepare. A tested rig and a paid course would make the choice concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the refresher need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a bound-bit stop, a power failure and the handover from robot to operator. A certificate without bound-bit and power-failure drills would not reassure me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop working at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare monthly pension income with our ordinary spending. If it comes up short, I would keep paid rig shifts or look at another local mine.

say: I see **2036 logs** changing before capable drill robots around 2039.
I want **tested rigs** and enough warning to choose full-shift retirement.
think: I hope to leave **full shifts** before robots arrive at 71.
I need **pension figures** before promising a retirement date despite strong savings.
do: **Keep** drilling on current shifts for now.
**Review** pension and savings each spring with my partner.
**Reduce** shifts after 2036 only if pension and savings cover bills.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work, with the retirement choice still tied to figures.
S4.quote: I would rather adjust a retirement plan than sell my partner a retirement date we cannot afford.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at capable robots makes retirement planning the chief issue.
**Eight months** saved and higher pay allow calm near-term choices without assuming a pension amount.
**Hands-on mentoring** remains important even in her long-horizon response.

steps.text: Keep drilling on current paid shifts for now
Wait to reduce shifts until pension and savings cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drill crew that thinking AI changes our logs by 2036 and capable drill robots come around 2039. A decade gives the mine time to test rigs and gives us time to decide when to leave full shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 when robots arrive. I would like to be off full shifts before then, and eight months of savings plus steady pay make planning possible. I still need to see the pension amount before promising my partner a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling for now and review our pension and savings each spring. In the first year after 2036 I would check whether the new log changes my work hours, then cut my shifts only if the pension and savings cover ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the near years. I can test small changes as they arrive and use actual household figures for the bigger decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my apprentice coworker Leena to learn the rig’s hard-seam feel while a person is beside her. The screen may help, but she needs a safe stop drilled into her hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep full rig shifts if my health allows and ask about openings at nearby mines. I would rather adjust a retirement plan than sell my partner a retirement date we cannot afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable drill robots around 2031 could reduce hours before the retirement date I had in mind. A paid rig trial, clear staffing plan and pension estimate would help me choose whether to stay or seek work at another mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the hard stops before anyone removes a drill operator. A bound bit is a real problem even when the screen looks calm.

headlineQuote: A bound bit is a real problem even when the screen looks calm.
portrait: **Grace, 58**, operates a drill rig and knows the feel of a bit crossing hard rock.
**Higher pay** and eight months of savings let her plan retirement, though pension income is still unconfirmed.
**Proven tools** appeal to her; she occasionally uses AI but checks orders against parts catalogues.
**Fast AGI** makes her anxious because capable drill robots around 2031 could reduce work before her chosen retirement.
**Longer warning** lets her seek paid refresher training and compare pension figures before reducing shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves the shortest time before capable drill robots may reduce her hours around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **A paid rig trial** and clear staffing plan would show what work remains.
**A pension estimate** would help her weigh fewer shifts against nearby mine jobs.
